query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy (HEA) multilayers under sustained loading, progressive plastic deformation is governed primarily by interface-mediated dislocation activity, specifically the nucleation and glide of dislocations at and across the heterophase interfaces, rather than by bulk dislocation motion within the layers. The high compositional complexity and lattice distortion in HEAs enhance resistance to dislocation motion within each phase, making the interfaces the dominant pathways for plasticity. This mechanism leads to a creep response that is more sensitive to interface structure and chemistry than to the intrinsic properties of the constituent bulk phases.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers, with coherent or semi-coherent interfaces, deposited on a suitable substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply sustained uniaxial load (constant stress) at elevated temperature within the stability range of the multilayer structure.
generation.conditions: Temperature and stress chosen to avoid phase transformation or gross interdiffusion, but sufficient to activate creep; multilayer period and overall thickness kept constant; comparison between multilayers with different interface structures (e.g., sharp vs. intermixed interfaces) or different HEA compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic structure and chemical complexity of the FCC/BCC interfaces, including degree of coherency, intermixing, and local short-range order.
generation.mechanism: Interfaces act as preferential sites for dislocation nucleation and glide due to the high resistance to dislocation motion within the highly distorted HEA layers. The local atomic disorder and possible short-range order at the interfaces modulate the activation energy for dislocation processes, controlling the creep rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayers with more coherent and chemically sharp interfaces will exhibit lower creep rates (higher creep resistance) than those with intermixed or incoherent interfaces, due to higher barriers for dislocation nucleation and transmission. The overall creep rate will be significantly lower than that of single-phase HEA films of comparable composition and thickness, and the deformation will localize at or near the interfaces.
generation.baseline: Creep rate and deformation mode of single-phase HEA thin films or conventional metallic multilayers (e.g., Ni/Nb) under similar loading and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis applies to nanoscale multilayers with stable FCC/BCC HEA phases, interface spacing below ~100 nm, and test conditions that do not induce phase instability or grain coarsening.
generation.uncertainty: Lack of direct experimental evidence for interface-mediated creep in HEA multilayers; possible contributions from grain boundary sliding or diffusion at very small layer thicknesses; unknown effects of specific alloy chemistries and interface structures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FCC/BCC HEA multilayers with systematically varied interface structures (e.g., by controlling deposition parameters to tune interface sharpness and coherency). Subject all samples to identical sustained loading at elevated temperature. Measure creep rates and analyze deformation microstructures using TEM and atom probe tomography.
measurements: Creep rate (strain vs. time under constant stress)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If multilayers with sharper, more coherent interfaces do not show lower creep rates than those with intermixed or incoherent interfaces, or if deformation is not localized at interfaces but instead occurs predominantly within the bulk of the layers, the hypothesis is falsified.
